name: Archimedes' principle
seoTitle: Archimedes' principle Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Archimedes' principle: work out acceleration due to gravity from the true mass of the object and the density of the object. A free physics calculator with…
summary: The surface area of the fluid and the Archimedes' principle calculator solves for acceleration due to gravity. The inputs are the true mass of the object, the density of the object, the apparent weight of the object. That makes it useful for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Archimedes' principle calculator work?
sections.html:
The Archimedes' principle calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports acceleration due to gravity in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the fluid type); then you type in the true mass of the object, the density of the object, the apparent weight of the object and the surface area of the fluid.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Archimedes' principle calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Acceleration due to gravity=-apparent weight of the object ÷ (volume of the object × (density of the fluid − density of the object))
Acceleration due to gravity=true weight of the object ÷ true mass of the object
Force of buoyancy=density of the fluid × acceleration due to gravity × volume of the fluid displaced
Volume of the object=true mass of the object ÷ density of the object
Density of the fluid=density of the object − apparent mass of the object ÷ volume of the object
Apparent mass of the object=-density of the fluid × volume of the fluid displaced + true mass of the object

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Volume, opening in cubic meters
  • Force, opening in newtons
  • Acceleration, opening in meters per second squared
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Force, opening in newtons
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Archimedes' principle calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the true mass of the object, the density of the object and the apparent weight of the object — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Archimedes' principle calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns acceleration due to gravity, derived from the true mass of the object, the density of the object and the apparent weight of the object. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Archimedes' principle calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the true mass of the object, the density of the object, the apparent weight of the object and the surface area of the fluid, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter true mass of the object in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. True mass of the object opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Density of the fluid = 0 kg/m³. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Archimedes' principle calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
